title: The Gift of Tongues
english: The wonders that God has in store for those who love Him are beyond human comprehension, as stated in the phrase 'the eye does not know, and the ear has not heard, and it has not come up into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love Him' (1 Corinthians 2:9).
The initial affliction that will befall them is characterized by the foolishness of lips and the use of a foreign tongue, which is a manifestation of God's power.

The mind of prophecy operates in a unique and distinct manner, as seen in the Acts of the holy apostles, where it is written that on the day of Pentecost, the disciples were all gathered in one place when a sound like a violent wind came from heaven, and then tongues of fire appeared, resting on each of the disciples.

The disciples began to speak in other languages as the Spirit gave them the ability to speak, saying 'tongues divided like fire appeared to them, and they sat on each one of them, and they began to speak in other tongues, as the Spirit gave them to speak' (Acts 2:3-4).

Prior to this event, Christ had commanded the disciples not to leave Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, until they were clothed with power from on high, which would enable them to fulfill their mission.

After receiving this power, the disciples spoke to people from various countries, including Israel, in the languages given to them by God, and the crowd was amazed, hearing them speak in their own languages, and they wondered how the disciples, who were Galileans, could speak in their own languages.
The crowd said, 'Are not all who speak Galileans? And how do we all hear them speaking in our own language?'

Others, however, mocked the disciples, saying they were drunk with sweet wine, that is, drunk, which illustrates the concept of the foolishness of lips and a foreign tongue, as foretold in the prophecy 'in foreign tongues and in other lips, I will speak to this people, and not even so will they believe'.

To accept the sign of the disciples' speaking in tongues with full assurance, one must consider the prior proclamation from God concerning this event, which the people had ignored, leading to their disobedience, and instead, they remained in disobedience, mocking the drunkenness.
They said, 'this rest is for the drinker, and this trampling, and they did not want to listen', demonstrating their rejection of God's message.

God said concerning the intentions of the Jews, 'Behold, I will bring a famine upon the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the Lord' (Amos 8:11), and as a result, the people would search for the word of God from east to west, but they would not find it.

This famine is a conceptual one, and it has been sent upon the people of Israel because they did not accept through faith the bread of life that came from heaven, giving life to the world, and instead, they have become needy of the food given by God.
It is written, 'man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God' (Deuteronomy 8:3), emphasizing the importance of spiritual nourishment.
Despite their wickedness, God calls the people to repentance, for He is good and is the Savior and Redeemer of all, demonstrating His love and mercy towards them.
translator_notes: The Greek text may be fragmented, and some sentences may be cut off at the beginning or end.

title: False Comfort
english: You take counsel and lift up a vain comfort, promising amnesty to those who have been provoked and saying that God will not be overly bitter toward them, having taken good counsel.
Yet you regard this vain comfort as something great and lofty, and so you are carried away beyond what is reasonable.

What is this great and useless comfort you consider? It is this: 'We will make a covenant with Hades and a pact with death; if a tempest comes, it will not come to us; we have made a lie our hope, and we will be sheltered by the lie.' (Isaiah 28:15)

But those who entertain these thoughts and cling to empty hope, imagining they will die before the terrible things they hear, will hear clearly: 'When the tempest comes, you will become a trampling for it. When it passes, it will seize you.' (Isaiah 28:18-19)
Woe to the city of Ariel, which David besieged! (Isaiah 29:1)

Gather your harvest year after year, yet you shall eat with Moab, for I will lay waste to Ariel; her strength and wealth shall be mine, and I will encamp against you like David, raising fortifications and setting up towers. (Isaiah 29:2-3)
Then your speech will be brought low, speaking from the ground, and your utterance will bow down to the dust. (Isaiah 29:4)
Your voice shall be like that of one calling from the earth, and your voice shall be weak towards the ground. (Isaiah 29:4)
Now Jerusalem was once called Jebus, and the blessed David captured it. (2 Samuel 5:6-7)

David went with all his men to Jerusalem against the Jebusite inhabitant of the land, and it was said to him: 'You shall not enter here,' because the blind and the lame had taken their stand, saying, 'He shall not enter here.' (2 Samuel 5:6)
Nevertheless, David captured the stronghold of Zion, which became the city of David. (2 Samuel 5:7)
On that day David declared: 'Whoever attacks a Jebusite, let him strike the blind and the lame with the sword, the soul of David.' (2 Samuel 5:8)
Thus the blessed David was opposed by the blind and the lame from Jerusalem or Jebus, and they were miserably overthrown.

He captured the city, yet later the inhabitants of Jerusalem—the blind and the lame—opposed the Savior Christ at the time of his visitation, because they did not know how to walk uprightly, nor did they receive the divine light into their mind…
translator_notes: The Greek source text appears fragmented at the beginning and end, with edge words possibly missing; rendered literally with ellipsis where incomplete.
The phrase os. at the start and the final fragment οἱ τὴ are edge fragments; no completion attempted.
Direct quotations from Isaiah and Samuel are translated fully into English as required; no Greek retained in main text.
The term ἐφ' οἷς πεπαρῳνήκασιν is rendered as 'those who have been provoked' based on contextual sense of prior irritation or stimulation leading to deserved amnesty.
The phrase ψυχὴν ∆αβίδ is translated as 'the soul of David' to match the Greek source.

title: Condemnation of Israel's Leaders
english: They are being tossed about again as lovers of sin and having become apostates from Israel, being very wicked and bitter in their counsels, and not through God. For it is not lawful to take counsel with God when one wishes to agree with some of the wicked. But one who is pious, good, and a lover of righteousness will take counsel with God and will turn toward practical things. For it is written, 'The thoughts of the righteous are judgments.'

Therefore, the chosen Israel is being accused, as having introduced a mind apostate from God concerning Christ. For they were inquiring, having gathered together, and said, 'What are we to do, since this man performs many signs? If we let him alone, the Romans will come and take away both your city and your land.' Another of the leaders said, 'You do not know anything, that it is expedient for one man to die, and not for the whole nation to perish.'

The Lord teaches this more clearly by saying in evangelical parables, 'The householder who planted the vineyard sent his own servants to receive the fruits, but the farmers killed them.' And their impieties have not stopped at these things; for having seen the son sent by the father along with the servants, they said to themselves, 'This is the heir; come, let us kill him and take his inheritance for ourselves.'

Thus, they are apostates, the proponents of such bitter and impious schemes, adding sin upon sin; for they killed the holy prophets, and then also the heir, that is, the son. Because their intention to apostatize from God is seen from afar, they attempt to make it certain by saying: 'Those going down to Egypt—they did not ask me to be a help under Pharaoh, or to be a shelter under the Egyptians.'

The sequence of these thoughts is this: Woe to those going down to Egypt to be helped by Pharaoh and to find shelter among the Egyptians. For having been informed of war and battle and the king of Assyria moving his weapons against the land of Judah, they ran to the Egyptians for help, calling for their assistance, even though they ought to have been appeasing God and turning toward better things. For if they had been enriched by his favor, they would not have been swept away by the forces of those making war...
translator_notes: The text begins mid-sentence with '...toward a people who will not benefit them...'; the final sentence is fragmentary, ending mid-clause.
